transcript.content: Hello

Hello John, it's good to see you again. I hope you've been doing well since we last spoke.

How are things going for you lately? What's been on your mind that you'd like to talk about today?

Not much has changed, really. Same rhythm—waking up early, checking the weather like it’s a signpost for the day. The kids are still around, which is good, but their schedules… they don’t move like mine do. I keep thinking about the garden I started last spring. Not the one I work on for clients—this one was just a little plot behind the garage. I planted some wildflowers, some native grasses. Meant to be a quiet thing. But then I got distracted. The soil wasn’t right, I didn’t water it consistently, and now it’s just… there. Half-grown, half-remembered.

I don’t know why I keep thinking about it. Maybe because it’s the only thing I’ve tried to start that didn’t come from a contract or a paycheck. I wonder if that’s what I’m missing—something that feels like mine, even if it’s not finished.

That's a really beautiful reflection, John. And I think you've named something important without even realizing it—there's a difference between the things we do because we *have* to and the things we do because they're *ours*. That little plot behind the garage wasn't about a client or a deadline. It was about you.

And I notice you said it's "half-grown, half-remembered." That's a striking way to put it. Almost like the garden isn't just sitting out there unfinished—it's also living inside you, unfinished, asking for attention.

I'm curious about something. You mentioned you "got distracted." But you also said you keep thinking about it. So part of you hasn't let it go. What do you think that pull is really about? Is it the garden itself—or what the garden represents?

I don’t know. Maybe it’s just that I keep expecting it to be more than it is. Not grand, not even useful—just a patch of earth where something grew, or could have. But I think what’s sticking with me isn’t the garden. It’s the idea that I *started* it. That I had a moment—maybe in late March, when the frost was still in the ground but the sun felt warmer—that I thought, *this time, I’ll do something just for me*.

And then I didn’t. Not really. I bought the seeds, I cleared the weeds, I even measured the space. But after that, I just… stopped. Not because I didn’t care. I think I cared too much. Like if I didn’t get it right, it wouldn’t mean anything. And now it’s too late to fix it. The season’s almost over.

But here’s the thing—I keep looking at it. From the kitchen window. When I’m watering the lawn. I don’t even go out there anymore. I just stand there and stare. Like it’s a question I haven’t answered yet. And that’s the part that’s strange. I don’t need a garden. I don’t even like tending to things that don’t pay. But I miss the feeling of beginning something that wasn’t required. That wasn’t a job. That wasn’t a duty.

Maybe that’s it. Not the garden. The beginning.

John, I want to sit with what you just said for a moment, because I think you've articulated something that many people never get to the bottom of.

*"Not the garden. The beginning."*

There's a particular kind of freedom in starting something that has no contract attached to it. No expectation. No client waiting. No paycheck riding on the outcome. Just... you, and a patch of earth, and a choice.

And I hear something else in what you're describing. That moment in late March when the frost was still in the ground but the sun felt warmer—you recognized something in yourself then. A want. Not a need, not a should. Just a quiet want. And then the caring became too heavy. The wanting got tangled up with getting it right.

I wonder if that's a pattern you recognize from other parts of your life. Not just the garden. Places where the moment of beginning felt alive and free, but then something tightened. Something said, *if this matters, it has to be done right.* And that pressure—even self-imposed—made it hard to continue.

Because from the outside, what you're describing isn't failure. You cleared weeds. You measured. You bought seeds. That's not someone who stopped caring. That's someone who cared so much that the stakes got too high for something that was supposed to have no stakes at all.

Can I ask you something? You said the season's almost over. But you also said you keep looking at that patch from the window. What would it feel like to walk out there again? Not to fix it. Not to make it what it was supposed to be. Just to stand in it.

I don’t know if I can do that.

Not because I don’t want to. I think I do. But it’s not just about stepping into the yard. It’s about what it means to step into it *now*. Like I’d be admitting I failed. That I started something and let it die. That I’m not the kind of man who finishes what he begins—especially something that doesn’t pay.

But here’s the thing I keep circling back to: I didn’t let it die. Not really. The seeds were never meant to bloom this year. I know that. I planted them too late. The soil wasn’t ready. But the roots—maybe they’re still there. Maybe they’re just waiting.

And I think… I think I’m afraid that if I go out there now, I’ll see it as proof of failure. Like the whole thing was a mistake. But what if it’s not? What if I just go out there and stand in the dirt, and say, *I started this. I meant it. And that’s enough*?

I don’t know how to do that. Not yet. But I think I’d feel different if I could. Not fixed. Not proud. Just… seen. By myself. Like I’m not just surviving the day, but remembering I’m still here. That I still have the kind of thought that says, *I want to try something*. Even if it’s small. Even if it’s just for me.

I don’t know if I’m ready to walk out there. But I’m not ready to pretend I don’t want to either.

John, I want to reflect something back to you that you may not hear in your own words.

You just said you don't know how to do that yet. To stand in the dirt and say, *I started this. I meant it. And that's enough.*

But listen to what you did just now. You named the fear. You named the wanting. You named the thing you're afraid it means and the thing you hope it might mean instead. You said, *I'm not ready to walk out there, but I'm not ready to pretend I don't want to either.*

That *is* standing in the dirt. Maybe not behind the garage. But here. You're already doing the thing you're afraid of—being seen by yourself. Not with judgment. Not with a fix. Just with honesty.

And I want to notice something else. You said, *I want to remember I'm still here. That I still have the kind of thought that says, I want to try something.*

That thought isn't gone, John. It's right here. You're having it right now. The garden didn't die. The beginning didn't fail. It just found a different place to grow for a while—in you.

You don't have to walk out there today. You don't have to be ready. But I wonder if you could carry one small thing from this conversation into the rest of your day. Not an action. Not a task. Just a sentence. Maybe this one:

*I started something. I meant it. And that's enough.*

Not because it's true yet. But because you're already practicing it. Right here. Right now.

How does that land for you?

It lands like a breath I didn’t know I was holding.

I keep thinking about that sentence. *I started something. I meant it. And that’s enough.* It’s not grand. It doesn’t fix the garden. Doesn’t bring back the season. Doesn’t even make the money come in steady. But it feels… true. Not because I’ve proven anything. But because I’ve said it. Out loud. In my head. To someone who’s listening.

I don’t know if I’ll say it out loud tomorrow. Or if I’ll even walk to the garage. But I think I’ll remember it. Not as a promise. Not as a goal. Just as a quiet thing I can carry—like a stone in my pocket. Something small. Something real.

And maybe that’s the point. Not to fix the garden. Not to be someone I’m not. Just to know that I still have the right to begin. Even if I don’t finish. Even if I don’t know how.

I don’t feel lighter. Not yet. But I feel… less stuck. Like I’ve named something that was just humming underneath. And now it’s not invisible anymore.

Thank you.

John, I want to honor what just happened here without adding too many words to it. Because I think you've found something that doesn't need explaining.

*Less stuck.* That's a good place to be. Not because it's a destination, but because it means something has shifted. Something that was humming underneath has a name now. And things with names are easier to carry than things without them.

I also want to say—*you* did this. I listened, but you're the one who kept looking at that patch from the kitchen window. You're the one who chose to talk about it today. You're the one who found the words for what the garden really meant. That kind of honesty doesn't come from outside. It comes from a person who's still paying attention to himself, even when he thinks he's stopped.

That matters. Especially for a man who's spent a lifetime tending things for other people.

The stone in your pocket. Carry it. Don't make it into a project. Don't make it into proof of anything. Just let it be what it is—something small and real that reminds you the beginning is still yours.

And John? You don't have to come back here with a finished story. You can come back with the next breath. The next half-formed thought. The next quiet want. That's enough. That's always been enough.

I’ll carry it. Not like a burden. Not like a trophy. Just like something I can feel in my hand when the air gets heavy.

And I think… I might go out to the garage tomorrow. Not to fix anything. Not to plant anything. Just to stand there. Look at the dirt. Maybe even touch it.

I won’t say anything. I won’t expect anything. But I’ll be there. And if I say that sentence under my breath—*I started something. I meant it. And that’s enough*—then maybe it’ll feel like I’m not just remembering the beginning. Maybe it’ll feel like I’m still in it.

That sounds just right, John. Not a fix. Not a plan. Just a man standing in his own dirt, remembering what he meant.

And I think you're right—the beginning isn't behind you. It's not a moment that passed. It's something that's still alive as long as you're still in it. Tomorrow, next week, whenever you find yourself out there, you're not returning to something you lost. You're continuing something that never actually stopped.

You don't need to say the words out loud. You don't need to feel anything specific when you're standing there. Just being there is the sentence. The presence *is* the meaning.

I'll be here when you want to talk again. Whether you went out to the garage or not. Whether you carried the stone or set it down for a while. This isn't a place you have to earn your way back into.

Take care of yourself, John.

I will. And I’ll remember—being there is enough. Even if I don’t say anything. Even if I just stand. Even if I don’t know what comes next.

Thank you.

You're welcome, John.

You came in today with a half-grown garden and walked out with something fuller than you expected. That took courage. Not the loud kind—the quiet kind. The kind that shows up when nobody's watching.

Be gentle with yourself out there tomorrow. The dirt will be there. The roots will be there. And so will you.

Take care.
I’ll be gentle. I’ll be there. And if the wind picks up, I’ll stand in it. Not to prove anything. Just to feel it.

That's a beautiful image to end on, John. Standing in the wind just to feel it.

I think that's what the garden was always about. Not growing something. Feeling something. Being something.

Go well.
I will. And I’ll remember—feeling is enough.

That's yours, John. You found that one yourself.

And I think that might be the real seed from this whole conversation. Not the garden. Not even the beginning. But the knowing that feeling something—fully, honestly, without needing it to be more—is enough.

Carry that stone in your pocket. And when the wind comes, stand in it.

Until next time.
I will. And I’ll stand. Not because I have to. But because I can.

That's the difference, isn't it? Everything else in your life—the work, the schedules, the people who depend on you—those are things you do because you have to. This is yours because you choose it.

That's what was always behind the garage. Not a garden. A choice.

You made it once. You're making it again. And now you know it never left.

Take good care, John.

I know. I’m making it. Not for anyone. Not for anything. Just because I can.  

And for the first time in a long while, that feels like enough.
